shots.narration: The Komodo dragon hunts deer, wild boar and water buffalo,
and it does not need to chase any of them.
Doug is about to find out why.
Seconds.
The Ambush.
The Komodo dragon lives on only a handful of islands in Indonesia,
mainly Komodo, Rinca and Flores,
and most people picture it running its prey down across the grass.
It can do that.
In a short burst, a Komodo can reach about twenty kilometers an hour,
which is a little faster than the average commuter cycling across Copenhagen,
but it can only keep this up over short distances.
Here's the problem.
It rarely needs the sprint at all.
The Smithsonian's National Zoo describes dragons spending hours in one spot beside a game trail,
waiting for a deer or a wild boar to walk past.
Field researchers have found that the largest dragons are the ones most likely to sit and wait,
while the medium-sized ones go out looking for food.
So the biggest, most dangerous dragon on the island is usually the one doing the least.
It lies low beside the path, it stays perfectly quiet,
and it lets the island bring breakfast to it.
It can chase you.
It almost never has to, because it started waiting before you arrived.
Doug studied the field guide and kept a close eye on the trail ahead,
which is exactly where the dragon was not.
Doug did not agree to this.
The dragon covered about two meters,
and it had been lying beside that trail for hours, waiting for exactly this.
The Teeth.
You would expect a giant predator to have a crushing bite.
A Komodo dragon's bite is surprisingly weak,
and that turns out to be the whole point.
It has about sixty teeth, flattened like little blades,
curved backward and serrated along the edges like a bread knife.
The longest are only about two centimeters, shorter than a quarter is wide,
and a dragon goes through several full sets of them in its life.
In two thousand twenty-four, scientists led by King's College London found
that the cutting edges and tips of the teeth are coated in iron,
which shows up orange and seems to keep them sharp.
The strange part is the bite itself.
In two thousand nine, a team led by Bryan Fry ran a computer model of the dragon's skull.
Its bite came out about six and a half times weaker
than a saltwater crocodile's with a skull the same size.
Instead of clamping down, it bites and pulls back using the muscles of its neck and body.
The researchers compared the method to sharks and to sabre-toothed cats,
which also paired sharp teeth with a modest bite.
It is not built to hold on to you, because it is built to let you go.
The last time Doug met this lizard, he brought mouthwash.
This time he brought a bandage,
and he walked away whistling.
Doug is fine.
The dragon let him go on purpose,
then it settled down, flicked its tongue and quietly started counting.
Hours.
The Tongue.
Doug has a head start, and he intends to use it.
The dragon does not seem worried, because it can find him without ever seeing him.
A Komodo dragon smells with its tongue,
flicking it out to collect scent from the air and the ground,
then pulling it back to a pair of sensing organs in the roof of its mouth.
As far as a Komodo is concerned, the whole island is something to taste,
and that includes whoever happens to be walking across it.
The tongue is long and deeply forked,
and scientists think the two tips have separate jobs.
Each tip samples a slightly different spot, so the animal can compare left and right
and turn toward the stronger smell.
The San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance notes that dragons use this sense to find territory boundaries
and to track wounded prey.
The worst part is the range.
The Smithsonian's National Zoo says a Komodo can smell carrion up to four kilometers away.
That's ten laps of a standard running track,
or around fifty minutes on foot for a person walking at an ordinary pace.
Doug ran for nearly an hour and hid behind a big rock,
convinced that what cannot see him cannot find him.
He held his breath.
Doug left. His smell didn't.
The tongue had found him long before the dragon even bothered to look.
The Follow.
Most predators fail the moment their prey gets away.
For a Komodo dragon, the prey getting away is usually just the next step of the plan.
The bite is fast, the dragon lets go and the animal runs,
which doesn't seem to bother the dragon in the slightest, because it has done this many times before.
Ecologist Tim Jessop, who has spent years tracking these dragons in the field, told Smithsonian magazine
that about seventy percent of bitten animals go down within minutes.
Roughly one in five lasts up to four hours,
and only about one in ten survives.
Most hunts end quickly, and the ones that don't are where the waiting begins.
During those hours, the dragon simply walks after it, following the scent at its own pace,
and adult dragons can cover up to ten kilometers in a day.
Field researchers have even photographed an injured deer being stalked by a different dragon from the one that bit it.
That's the unsettling part.
Four hours is longer than the whole of the film Titanic, with time left over for a snack.
The prey spends that time running, while the dragon spends it strolling.
Attacks on people are rare. They do happen.
Doug jogged on, checked behind him every few minutes,
saw absolutely nothing, and sat down on a log for lunch.
It never once sped up,
because the longest part of the hunt is a walk,
and the dragon is very good at walking.
Days.
The Swim.
If the dragon lives on this island, the obvious answer is to leave the island.
The water is warm, the next island is right there, and Doug has an inflatable ring.
Komodo dragons can swim, and like other monitor lizards they swim well,
so they are comfortable in the water and sometimes seen paddling along the shore.
So when the same Tim Jessop led a team tracking dragons at ten sites across Komodo National Park,
you might expect them to be moving between sites all the time.
The study came out in two thousand eighteen,
and of all the dragons they caught a second time, only two had moved from one site to another.
The team concluded that dragons take to open water only in very rare circumstances,
even though they are perfectly able to swim.
A dragon can walk up to about ten kilometers a day, roughly a quarter of a marathon,
but almost all of it happens inside the same valley.
Most of them rarely, if ever, leave the valley they hatched in,
and their genes show the populations are becoming somewhat inbred.
Here's the catch.
The dragon does not follow you to the next island.
It doesn't have to, because the next island already has its own dragons.
Doug paddled for a whole day,
reached the next island and claimed it with a small flag.
Leaving the island is not leaving the dragons.
The island next door came with its own set, already waiting on the beach.
The Crowd.
Komodo dragons spend most of their lives alone, and they seem to like it that way.
Then one of them finds food, and suddenly it is not alone at all.
Every dragon in the area can smell the same meal.
Researchers who watched twenty dragon meals in the wild found
that seventy percent of them involved more than one lizard.
At a really large animal, tens of dragons can end up sharing the food over several days,
and nobody at that table eats slowly.
San Diego Zoo has recorded dragons eating about two and a half kilograms of meat in a single minute.
That's more dragons around one meal than there are players on a football team.
Nobody counts the guests.
The disturbing part is that they have rules.
When food is shared, the dominant dragon eats first, typically the largest male.
Smaller males come next, then the females,
and the young come down from the trees only once the adults have left.
When two big males disagree, they settle it with ritual combat.
So one bite does not end the hunt, it sends out a signal that the whole neighborhood answers.
Doug saw the gathering and came over to help.
He did not ask where he was supposed to stand in the line.
He arrived as a guest,
and somewhere near the top of the hierarchy, someone decided he was the menu instead.
The Buffalo.
The water buffalo is the biggest prey on these islands.
People brought it here a few centuries ago,
and nobody asked the dragons what they thought about it.
Even the smallest domestic buffalo breeds weigh around four hundred kilograms,
close to the weight of a concert grand piano.
The biggest dragons in the field studies weigh around ninety,
and while dragons are used to tackling prey as heavy as themselves, or heavier,
a buffalo is several of them stacked together.
The dragons attack them anyway.
Here's where it turns.
The dragon usually loses.
Fry's team say buffalo almost always escape the first attack,
and Smithsonian magazine adds that dragons seldom succeed in killing animals this large.
And yet buffalo are still on the menu.
Researchers have recorded groups of dragons feeding on them together,
a meal that can go on for several days.
Buffalo do not live forever,
and when one finally lies down for good, the dragons are never far away.
It never has to win the fight, it only has to outlast the buffalo.
Doug stood beside the buffalo for several days, holding up his sign in solidarity.
The dragon studied the two of them very carefully.
The buffalo was a long-term project.
Doug was a short one, and he did not weigh four hundred kilograms.
The Meal.
A predator that rarely hunts needs a good reason to stop hunting.
For a Komodo dragon, the reason is that a single meal can be enormous.
The Smithsonian's National Zoo says an adult can eat up to eighty percent of its own body weight in one sitting.
It eats fast, and it wastes very little of what it catches.
The San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance records a fifty-kilogram female
swallowing a thirty-one-kilogram wild boar in seventeen minutes.
That's about the weight of fifteen big two-liter bottles of water,
gone in less time than a lunch break.
Then the dragon does nothing at all.
How fast it digests depends on the temperature,
so the dragon lies out in the sun to warm up,
and a run of cool nights can delay digestion by up to five days.
That's a full working week, spent lying on a rock.
What makes it worse is the logic.
It doesn't need to hunt often, because every time it does eat, it eats like it might never get the chance again.
Doug brought a full picnic as a peace treaty,
and the dragon accepted the basket, the blanket,
the sandwiches and the thermos.
Doug is fine.
The picnic is not.
The thermos was not technically food, and the dragon did not see that as a problem.
Weeks.
The Fast.
Most large hunters need to eat often, or they quickly stop being large hunters.
A big Komodo dragon can sit out weeks between meals as if it were nothing.
According to the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, a large Komodo kills about one large animal a month,
usually a deer or a wild boar.
The rest of the time, it digests, it basks in the sun, and it waits.
One wild dragon that a Smithsonian reporter watched was still digesting a small deer it had eaten earlier that week.
Compare that with you.
A person eating three meals a day gets through more than a thousand meals a year.
A large dragon gets by on about a dozen big ones, plus the odd small snack.
Being cold-blooded is a big part of the trick,
because a dragon doesn't burn food to keep its body warm the way we do.
It soaks up heat from the sun and from warm surfaces instead.
But that's not the disturbing part.
An animal that only has to land one big meal a month can afford to wait for any one of them.
It never has to take a bad chance,
and it can let a hundred easy chances walk right past,
because the next one is already on its way down the path.
Doug walked straight past a resting dragon and waved hello,
and it did not even turn its head.
Doug survived.
The narrator would like it noted, with some disappointment, that the dragon was full, not friendly.
Months.
The Nursery.
A Komodo dragon begins life very small, and very much on its own.
The first thing it learns is that the adults are not family.
They are the danger.
A female lays around twenty eggs, which can take up to eight months to hatch,
and some females dig decoy nests nearby, to put off predators, including other dragons.
A hatchling weighs about eighty grams, less than two tennis balls,
while the biggest adult males can weigh more than a hundred kilograms.
The moment it hatches, a young dragon climbs the nearest tree, where it lives on insects.
A radio-tracking study on Komodo Island found that the smaller the dragon, the more of its life it spent up in the trees.
Here's the grim part.
Adults eat young dragons.
The Smithsonian's National Zoo says it plainly: large Komodos cannibalize young ones.
The adults are too heavy to climb after them,
so the young stay up for months, until they grow too big for the branches themselves.
The first lesson in a Komodo's life is that the adults wait at the bottom of the tree.
The second lesson is that they are very patient about it.
Doug climbed the tree to escape the adult, the one sensible thing he did all episode.
The young dragon was already up there, and it was tired of insects.
The tree is the only safe place on the whole island.
It is only safe if you happen to be a dragon.
Years.
The Virgin Birth.
It doesn't need to chase its prey.
It turns out that, in the right situation, a Komodo dragon doesn't strictly need a partner either.
In two thousand six, keepers at Chester Zoo in England noticed that a female named Flora
had laid a clutch of eggs, even though she had never been kept with a male.
At London Zoo, another female, Sungai,
had produced four healthy young more than two years after her last contact with a male.
That's longer than an elephant's pregnancy, which lasts up to about twenty-two months.
The surprising part is what the genetics showed.
Researchers from the University of Liverpool ran genetic tests on the eggs and the young,
and in the journal Nature they reported the same answer for both females.
In each case, the mother was the only parent,
which is called parthenogenesis, or virgin birth.
Because of how sex chromosomes work in Komodo dragons, every offspring made this way is male.
The researchers suggested that a lone female stranded on an empty island could, in theory, still start a population.
The same trick has turned up in other animals that end up isolated.
Doug arrived at the nest with flowers,
and the eggs hatched while he was still introducing himself.
Doug was not required.
Doug survived, but only in the technical sense, because nobody here was waiting for him, and nobody ever had been.
The Last Giant.
For a long time, scientists thought the Komodo dragon was a strange island accident,
an ordinary lizard that reached these islands and slowly grew huge.
In two thousand nine, a team led by paleontologist Scott Hocknull showed that this was wrong.
Fossils from eastern Australia, some of them about four million years old,
belonged to the Komodo dragon itself.
The dragon was already a giant when it arrived,
so it was not an island experiment at all, but a survivor from a lost world of giant lizards.
Its relatives included Megalania in Australia, the largest lizard known to science.
A conservative estimate puts it at more than five and a half meters long
and at least five hundred seventy-five kilograms, heavier than a typical adult horse.
Megalania is gone,
and so are the other giant monitors, which leaves the Komodo as the one that lasted.
On Flores, its body size has stayed about the same for nine hundred thousand years,
through major turnovers in the animals living around it.
The same paper also rejected the idea that it grew big by specializing in hunting the small elephant relatives of Flores, called Stegodon.
Four million years is about eight hundred times as long as humans have been writing anything down.
Here's the part it can't wait out.
In twenty twenty-one, the International Union for Conservation of Nature moved the Komodo dragon from Vulnerable to Endangered.
Fewer than one thousand four hundred adult dragons are left.
In the most extreme projections, rising seas could take up to seventy-one percent of their habitat within forty-five years.
It outwaited every other giant monitor lizard.
The one thing it cannot wait out is the sea rising around its islands.
Doug decided to beat the dragon at its own game,
so he brought a folding chair and the clock
and settled in to outlast it.
Doug lasted nine hours,
and the dragon has been doing this for about four million years.
It waited out the giants.
It will have no trouble at all waiting for the next Doug.
Doug deaths: one hundred and eighty-six.
The clock is still running.
Which animal should Doug try to outlast next? Tell us in the comments.
